items.stem: Why does Rust require Arc rather than Rc to share ownership across threads?

options.text: Arc uses atomic reference counting so the count is safe under concurrent access
options.rationale: Arc's atomic counter is Send+Sync; Rc's non-atomic counter is not thread-safe.

options.text: Rc is faster and therefore preferred across threads
options.rationale: Rc is non-atomic and not thread-safe, so it is rejected across threads.
Arc does not affect borrow checking.

options.text: Rc cannot allocate on the heap
options.rationale: Rc also heap-allocates; the difference is atomicity.

items.explanation: Arc's atomic counter is Send+Sync; Rc's non-atomic counter is not thread-safe.

items.stem: Select TWO statements that correctly describe unsafe Rust.

options.text: unsafe lets you dereference raw pointers and call unsafe functions
options.rationale: These operations are only permitted inside unsafe.

options.text: unsafe disables all compiler borrow checking in the whole program
options.rationale: unsafe only unlocks specific operations; normal checks still apply.

options.text: Code in unsafe should uphold invariants so a safe wrapper can be sound
options.rationale: The point of unsafe is to build sound safe abstractions.

options.text: unsafe code is exempt from the type system
options.rationale: Type checking still applies inside unsafe.

items.explanation: These operations are only permitted inside unsafe.

items.stem: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism in an async Rust program?

options.text: Concurrency interleaves tasks; parallelism runs them on multiple cores at once
options.rationale: Async gives concurrency; parallelism needs multiple threads/cores.
They are distinct concepts even if related.
Rust supports parallelism via threads and multi-threaded runtimes.

items.explanation: Async gives concurrency; parallelism needs multiple threads/cores.
